scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance dates back over a thousand years to the warring Kshatriya clans of Kumaon.
It transitioned from a literal martial practice during the era of the Chand Kings in the 10th century into a ceremonial tradition that persists in modern marriage processions.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Primarily performed at weddings to protect the groom and bride from evil spirits and demons, it is now performed at various auspicious occasions.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Eight dancers perform in a synchronized manner, engaging in mock duels with tulwar swords and brass shields.
The performance includes carrying a triangular red flag called the nishana and maintaining facial expressions of warriors heading to battle.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is war-like, featuring brass instruments (turi, nagphani, ransing), percussion (dhol, damau), bagpipes (masakbeen), and woodwinds (nausuriya muruli, jyonya).
Listen for the turi, nagphani, ransing, dhol.
War-like music characterized by the sound of brass horns, bagpipes, and native drums.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear white churidar payajamas, a chola, a taanka headpiece, and apply sandalwood paste to their faces.
They carry tulwar swords and brass shields.
on_screen: Image gallery: 2 licensed images with attribution

scenes.title: The people
narration: Forms include Bisu nritya, Saraanv, Rann Nritya, Sarankar, Veerangna, Depanshu, Chholiya Baja, Shauka Shaili, and Paitan Baja.
Rooted in the martial traditions of the Kumaoni people and the Kshatriya clans of the 10th century.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The dance is performed as an apotropaic ritual to protect wedding processions from malevolent spirits and demons.
